title: How To Handle Students Who Question Your Classroom Management nagement/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin advises teachers on responding when a student challenges a classroom rule or procedure, often in front of the whole class. He warns that reacting with defensiveness or frustration is a mistake because it creates a you-against-them dynamic that can spread to the entire class. Instead, he recommends answering the question calmly and cheerfully with a brief, prepared explanation—such as "we raise our hands so everyone gets a fair chance to participate"—and then simply moving on without waiting for a rebuttal. He stresses that every rule, procedure, and routine needs a clear, logical purpose that a teacher can articulate in a sentence or two; unexplained or arbitrary expectations breed resentment. Coaching teachers, he says he frequently asks them why they do something and finds many cannot answer, which means their students cannot either. Knowing and communicating the 'why' behind classroom practices, he concludes, builds trust and prevents students from viewing teachers as arbitrarily bossy.
points: When students question a classroom rule, reacting with frustration or defensiveness creates a 'you-against-them' dynamic with the whole class.
The recommended response is to answer calmly and cheerfully with a brief, prepared explanation and then move on without waiting for a rebuttal.
Every rule, procedure, and routine should have a purpose the teacher can state clearly in a sentence or two.
In coaching sessions, Linsin often finds teachers cannot explain the purpose behind their own practices, meaning their students don't know it either.
Students don't need to agree with a rule, but they do need to know why it exists in order to trust the teacher and avoid resentment.
quotes: So when a student questions the way you manage your classroom—most often in front of the class—it can be hard not to take it personally. It can be hard not to bristle and become defensive.
Because showing frustration puts you at odds with not only the student who asked the question but with your entire class.
You calmly, even cheerfully, say your line and then move on. There is no reason to wait for a response or gird yourself for an argument.
If you can’t point to a logical reason why you have certain rules, procedures, routines, etc., then you’re asking for trouble. Because arbitrary or unexplained regulation causes resentment.
In my role coaching teachers , I find myself asking frequently “Why are you doing that? What’s the purpose?” And often they can’t tell me, which means their students don’t know either.
They don’t necessarily even have to agree. They just need to know why .
